The predominant scientific view, expressed by NASA [d1, d10], the EPA [d14], Yale Climate Connections [d9], Snopes citing climate researchers [d12], and the University of Hawaii [d13], is that melting sea ice does not meaningfully contribute to sea level rise, because floating sea ice already displaces roughly the same volume of water as it adds when it melts — analogous to an ice cube in a glass of water. As NASA states, "Sea Ice Melt Does Not Greatly Contribute to Sea Level Rise" [d10], and a climate researcher quoted by Snopes affirms: "Melting sea ice does not contribute directly to sea level rise as floating ice is already displacing its volume; no climate scientist would claim otherwise" [d12]. However, a competing scientific position exists: NSIDC reports research by Dr. Peter Noerdlinger (Noerdlinger & Brower, 2007) demonstrating that because freshwater meltwater is less dense than saltwater, melting sea ice and floating ice shelves could add approximately 2.6% more water to the ocean than the volume they displaced, equivalent to roughly 4 centimeters of sea-level rise [d2], a finding also discussed on Skeptical Science [d6]. Thus, while the mainstream consensus holds that sea ice melt has negligible direct impact on sea level, a minority scientific argument based on freshwater-saltwater density differences suggests a small but non-zero contribution [d2, d6].
